70e17b570179a526: IPOH: The Taiping Municipal Council (MPT) has rejected allegations of neglect and abuse involving three elephants transferred to a Japanese zoo, saying their behaviour does not necessarily indicate mental distress.
Its president, Mohamed Akmal Dahalan, said the elephants — Dara, Amoi and Kelat — were in good health and had adapted well to their new surroundings since arriving in Japan in March.
He said the latest reports from the zoo, alongside MPT's assessment, showed that all three elephants were active and in satisfactory overall condition.
"The three elephants have also been reunited since Sept 20 and have unrestricted access to the entire exhibition area and their night enclosures," he said in a statement.

Akmal said MPT took note of concerns raised on social media over the elephants' head-swaying behaviour, alleged zoochosis and the frequency of musth episodes, which had prompted questions about their mental and emotional well-being.

"In this regard, MPT wishes to reiterate that such behaviour should not be directly interpreted as signs of stress, depression or compromised animal welfare. MPT also denies any allegations of neglect or abuse involving the elephants.
"Head-swaying, in particular, cannot be directly interpreted as a sign of stress, as it may also indicate food-anticipation behaviour, in which an animal anticipates being fed," he said.
On Kelat's musth episodes, Akmal said the elephant had entered the phase twice since arriving in Japan, in May and September this year.
He acknowledged that Kelat had lost weight during both episodes but said this was normal. Its weight had since increased and was approaching the level recorded before the second episode in September.
Akmal also dismissed allegations that hormones had been injected into Kelat to increase the frequency of its musth episodes, describing the claims as untrue.
He said all three elephants were given a complete and balanced diet tailored to their nutritional needs, prepared by the zoo's animal care team and monitored by veterinary officers.

"Their diet includes hay, bamboo shoots, fresh grass, vegetables, specially formulated elephant pellets, alfalfa cubes, wheat bran, carrots, sweet potatoes, bread, pineapple tops and fruits such as apples. Salt and vitamins are also given daily," he said.
Akmal said Kelat had gained 580kg since arriving in Japan, while Dara had gained 575kg and Amoi 405kg.
He said the weight gains indicated that their food intake and health were satisfactory.
"Tennoji Zoo also conducts regular enrichment programmes involving varied activities, food and feeding methods to support the elephants' welfare and mental well-being," he added.
Akmal said the zoo remained committed to ensuring that the elephants' nutrition, veterinary care, safety and daily management complied with international standards and best practices.
While respecting the public's right to voice concerns, he urged people to ensure that allegations about the elephants' welfare were supported by credible information and professional assessments.
He said unsubstantiated claims could cause misunderstandings and potentially affect the country's conservation efforts and international cooperation.
"MPT will continue monitoring the elephants' health and welfare and providing updates to ensure the public receives accurate information," he added.

698fbb41068821fb: RIYADH: Saudi state oil company Aramco has told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf, six people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters on Thursday, as fighting between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensifies.

Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the group pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb, a shipping ​chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth.

The instruction to staff to evacuate the building and work remotely follows a wave of Houthi attacks on the kingdom, targeting the company and Saudi airports. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment on what would be the first evacuation since the start of the Iran war.
It was unclear what the reason for the evacuation was.

The kingdom's benchmark index TASI dropped 2.5 per cent on Thursday following the Aramco news, according to LSEG data. Oil prices rose to their highest since May on Thursday on concern over an escalation of the Middle East conflict and its impact on crude oil supplies from the world's key exporting region.
HOUTHIS SAY THEY TARGETED ARAMCO IN YANBU

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a televised speech that the group had launched attacks on Aramco facilities in the Red Sea city of Yanbu and the Saudi defence ministry in the capital Riyadh. Saudi authorities did not confirm the attack.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Thursday it had intercepted drones over Riyadh and Islam's holy city of Madinah, which is near Yanbu.

The renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and Houthi militias in recent weeks ended a 2022 UN-brokered truce, which had largely halted cross-border attacks, and opened another front ​in the US-Israeli ⁠war on Iran.
The Houthis caused extensive damage to Aramco's headquarters earlier this month when they struck the building, with fire spreading across several floors.
Saudi Arabia has responded to Houthi attacks with a wave of strikes on missile launcher sites, vowing to protect the kingdom, and says it has intercepted many ballistic missiles fired by the group.

Saree said that Saudi attacks on Yemen have killed and wounded 562 people since mid July, when the Houthis imposed a naval blockade on the kingdom which then drew a warning from the Saudi-led coalition that it ​would respond "firmly."

Separately, he said earlier on Thursday that the group is rescuing a boat carrying 14 Indians that was attacked off Jabal Zuqar island near the strait, one of the territories the group seized in an advance in September.
Saree blamed the attack on Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
HOUTHI AIRPORT ATTACKS

A Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Saudi Arabia's eastern oil hub of Dammam near Dhahran on Wednesday evening killed two people, a Saudi citizen and an Indian national, and wounded eight others.
Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Thursday that operations at the airport had resumed and air traffic had returned to normal.
The ​Houthis had warned airlines this month against using Saudi airspace ⁠as they have repeatedly targeted Saudi airports, including Riyadh's international airport and the southern airport of Abha.
Brent crude futures LCOc1 climbed US$3.06, or 2.81 per cent, to US$111.88 a barrel by 1104 GMT on Thursday. They hit US$112.55 a barrel earlier in the session, the highest since May 18.--REUTERS

ccdf273f1786a947: PUTRAJAYA: The Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi), and 22 others have appealed against a High Court ruling ordering them to pay lawyer and activist Siti Kasim RM160,000 in damages over her wrongful arrest and detention in 2016.

Senior Federal Counsel Ng Siew Wee, representing Jawi, 15 of its officers and seven others, said the appeal centred on three main issues: the element of mens rea (guilty intent) in misfeasance in public office, the allegation of malicious prosecution, and the judge's assessment of witness testimony and records from earlier criminal proceedings.
On the alleged misfeasance in public office, Ng argued that an honest mistake of law by the officers should not automatically be treated as an abuse of power.
"The evidence clearly shows that the motive behind the raid was to enforce the fatwa.
"An honest mistake of law does not constitute misfeasance in public office," she said.

On malicious prosecution, Ng argued that there was insufficient evidence to show that the Jawi enforcement officers who lodged the police report had acted dishonestly to have Siti Kasim charged with obstructing a public servant in the discharge of his duties.
She also argued that the High Court judge had erred in assessing a defendant's testimony and relying on records from an earlier criminal case as substantive evidence in determining liability.
Meanwhile, lawyer A. Saha Deva, representing Siti Kasim, whose full name is Siti Zabedah Kasim, argued that the High Court had properly considered the facts and applied the law.

He said the enforcement officers had proceeded with the raid without properly considering whether they had the legal authority to do so, demonstrating the mens rea required to establish misfeasance in public office.
"They did not care whether they had the authority or not; they proceeded with the raid regardless," he said.
Saha Deva said trial evidence showed that the officers continued with the raid even after Siti Kasim questioned whether their actions had a legal basis.
He also defended the High Court's findings on misfeasance in public office, saying the officers' conduct had to be assessed in light of the evidence as a whole.
A three-member panel chaired by Datuk Noorin Badaruddin fixed Nov 5 for case management to determine the date for its decision on the appeal.
The other judges on the panel were Datuk Dr Shahnaz Sulaiman and Datuk Meor Hashimi Abdul Hamid.

Siti Kasim filed the civil suit in September 2019 over her alleged wrongful arrest and detention during a raid by Jawi officers at a private fundraising dinner on April 3, 2016. She was subsequently taken to the Dang Wangi district police headquarters.
She claimed the actions amounted to false imprisonment, misfeasance in public office and a violation of her constitutional right to personal liberty.
She maintained that she had been acting in her capacity as a lawyer and had neither obstructed the officers in carrying out their duties nor committed any offence.
Siti Kasim also argued that Jawi had no jurisdiction or investigative powers over offences under the Penal Code.
On July 18, 2025, High Court Judge Su Tiang Joo ordered the defendants to pay RM100,000 in exemplary damages, RM60,000 in aggravated damages, and RM100,000 in legal costs to Siti Kassim.

The court held that Siti Kasim had proven on the balance of probabilities that she was wrongfully arrested and falsely imprisoned by two Jawi officers after exiting the ballroom of the hotel where the event was held.

ce2a77e6ae8a20da: GREENVILLE, Oct 22 — Young students attending their debut political gathering, longtime supporters coming since 2015, or curious onlookers witnessing a presidential spectacle, they all agree: as Donald Trump runs his final campaign, no one will be able to replace his rallies.
“There’s a lot of Americana. There’s a lot of, you know, happy people,” a Trump fan named Bart said Tuesday night’s outdoor campaign event in Greenville, North Carolina.
Trump has been barnstorming across multiple US states ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, with his party at serious risk of losing their majorities in Congress.
In this rural corner of the eastern United States, “we don’t have stuff like this happen very often,” said Bart, attending with his wife Courtney and their two children, ages 10 and 12.
Bart, who declined to give his last name, walked past a “MAGA” souvenir stand and rows of red, white and blue bunting before finding his seat on an airport tarmac where the rally was held.
It was a familiar feeling. He attended his first Trump campaign event in 2015.

Since then, millions of Americans have experienced this in-person ritual—a unique blend of provocative verbal attacks, consummate showmanship, and tireless enthusiasm, all from a president who has reached age 80.
Low-flying Air Force One
For 18-year-old Jaycie Bullard, dressed in Republican red, attending the rally was a no-brainer.
“When I heard that he was coming to Greenville, I knew I had to come,” said the nursing student enrolled at a nearby university.
“It’s pure joy, I feel like a little kid on Christmas.”
After an hours-long wait, a plane flew low overhead: Trump had arrived. He strode onstage to the strains of “God Bless the USA,” which has become a core part of his political events.

The president launched fierce attacks—sometimes tinged with racist overtones—against his opponents, claimed against all evidence that he won the 2020 election, and cracked oft-repeated jokes before he yielded the stage to a local Republican US Senate candidate.
His rambling, repetitive Greenville speech clocked in at 111 minutes. As always, he left the stage to the Village People’s “Y.M.C.A.”
But these moments, celebrated by the “Make America Great Again” faithful, are the vestiges of a fading political traveling roadshow that only Trump has been able to pull off.
The crowds and venues are getting smaller. Trump, constitutionally barred from a third term, must step down in January 2029.
“I’m nervous for the future,” admitted retiree Patty Laronde, who was seeing Trump for the first time.
“Who’s going to take his place?” she said. “I’m hopeful with JD Vance,” the vice president widely seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate.
Turning politics into ‘entertainment’

Even if another such master of ceremonies emerges in American politics, David, a self-employed 51-year-old, vocalized what many attendees were likely thinking: “the copy is never as good as the original.”
“He is an anomaly,” added Troy, 59, a manager who also did not give his last name. “There’s... never been a president like him,” he added, “and I don’t know there ever will be again.”
Researchers contacted by AFP tended to agree.

By “turning political rallies into entertainment,” Trump “takes alleged negative emotions such as resentment, grievance and disappointment and transforms them into excitement, pride and positive anticipation,” explained Yagmur Karakaya, a sociology professor at Yale University.
He relies on improvised comedy and culture-war jabs, sports metaphors, the ever-present “winning” philosophy, and business jargon, weaving it into a unique style.
“Can others do this? I am not so sure,” Karakaya said.

That is the million-dollar question, said speech communication professor Jacob Justice of the University of Mississippi, who likened a Trump rally’s atmosphere to that of “a Grateful Dead concert (or) a college football tailgate.”
If anyone could inspire something similar, he or she “might come from the world of social media influencing or podcasting,” Justice said.
Should that person be JD Vance, rallygoer Bart said, “he would bring half of these people.” — AFP
40dd9b0c9bd1f9a2: VARGEM GRANDE, Oct 22 — The first time he ate his fill, Walter dos Santos was 25 years old and had long since watched siblings die of hunger in northeastern Brazil, where they grew up without electricity, education, or prospects.
He learned to read and write and finished high school at 32. Today, his daughter holds a doctorate in biotechnology and his son is an agronomist.
The 56-year-old, who lives in Maranhao state, credits one man: Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Dos Santos said Lula was the “father and the mother and the grandfather” of Quilombo Piqui da Rampa—a traditional Afro-Brazilian community descended from enslaved people.
“Everything we were denied, our children can now have,” thanks to Lula’s social policies, he told AFP from his painted yellow house, a far cry from the mud-and-thatch-roofed structure he grew up in.
“Even if people call it handouts, for us they were an enormous help. Because anyone who has ever gone hungry knows not to take these programs for granted.”
His gratitude reflects Lula’s enduring appeal in Brazil’s vast Northeast, where he won nearly 64 percent of votes in a first-round election.
However, he lost over 250,000 votes compared to a 2022 election, which experts say is a sign voters are starting to look beyond social programs to improve their lives.
Nationally, Lula suffered a major blow as right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro defied polls to come out ahead. The pair face a tight runoff on Sunday.
A little ball of rice

Maranhao stretches from the Amazon rainforest to the Atlantic coast, where turquoise lagoons shimmer between the sweeping white dunes of Lencois Maranhenses. Once a major exporter of sugar and cotton, its economy built on enslaved labor, the state is now Brazil’s poorest.

Residents in communities around the city of Vargem Grande told AFP that before Lula first came to power in 2003, theirs was a hardscrabble life of subsistence farming and working in exchange for sugar, tobacco or cachaca (a Brazilian spirit).
“Mom would cook a single kilo of rice to feed everyone. She’d just take a small portion—a little ball of rice—for herself to eat,” said Dos Santos, who was one of 16 children.
Thick groves of babassu palms cover the landscape, for generations providing backbreaking work for women, who crack open the plants’ nuts to extract seeds used to make oil.

Residents of the region credit social programs championed by Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva with reducing poverty and expanding access to education, helping maintain his strong electoral support in Brazil's Northeast ahead of the presidential runoff election. — AFP pic
Maria de Fatima Mendes Ferreira, 54, who lives in the nearby Padre Trindade community, recalls losing her six-month-old baby—one of nine children—to malnutrition in her twenties.
“Back then, we didn’t eat properly. We worked all day long” cracking coconuts.

Her husband, fisherman Antonio Carlos Lima Ferreira, 51, said programs like Lula’s Bolsa Familia—which provides cash to low-income families who keep their children in school and vaccinated—had changed their life.
Lula “has a genuine love for the poor. That’s the crux of it.”
Programs that help locals sell their produce to the government, which in turn uses it to provide school meals and help families in need, have transformed these communities.
Beyond basic necessities
Vitor Hugo Miro, a researcher at the Brazilian Institute of Economics, said the poverty rate—below 775 reais ($154) a month—dropped from 67 percent to 49 percent in Maranhao between 2012 and 2025.
But he said economic opportunity and good jobs are limited, and people are increasingly worried about security as major criminal factions have expanded in the region.
While social programs have been crucial, “people are beginning to weigh other dimensions of their lives when deciding how to vote,” Miro said.

In the regional seaside capital Sao Luis, known for its colonial Portuguese architecture, crumbling tiled facades and cobbled streets, Larissa Bianque, 32, told AFP she was the only one in her family voting for Bolsonaro.
While much of her family depends on Bolsa Familia and other benefits, she said young people “aspire to something beyond just the aid that covers basic necessities.”
Quintessential Northeasterner
For Lula supporters, his life story growing up dirt poor is key to his appeal and gave a sense of pride to a region often mocked as backward and uneducated.
“He is the quintessential Northeasterner... yet he never forgot his roots,” said Zacarias Neto de Moraes, 58, a coordinator with Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT).
He spoke to AFP on the sidelines of a meeting discussing how to deal with a record abstention rate in the region.
“There is a segment of society made up of young people who never lived through the time before Lula. They don’t know what things were like back then,” he said. — AFP
df18d7b7a2f7a11d: JERUSALEM, Oct 22 — When Israel goes to the polls this month, voters will weigh in on military conscription, the economy and how the state should investigate its inability to prevent Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack.
AFP looks at the key issues shaping the campaign as Israel gears up for elections on October 27.
Accountability for October 7
Many Israelis have demanded an independent state commission of inquiry into the failures that allowed Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which resulted in the deaths of more than 1,200 people.
The deadliest day in Israel’s history, it inflicted a profound national trauma whose repercussions continue to shape the country’s politics, society and collective psyche.

Israel has launched commissions of inquiry after previous national crises, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main challenger in the upcoming poll, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, has pledged to do so again, calling it “a way to prevent the next disaster”.
But Netanyahu’s government, which was in office when the attack occurred, has rejected the calls.
Instead, it has blamed the security establishment for failing to prevent the assault and proposed a bipartisan commission whose members would be appointed by politicians.
Opposition figure Yair Lapid said the government-proposed commission’s purpose “is to whitewash (those responsible) and prevent a genuine investigation”.
Netanyahu himself has faulted the security services for not waking him sooner on the day of the attack.
He faces mounting accusations that he ignored early warnings—notably from the UAE, which reportedly told him Hamas was planning a major operation.

The premier has also come under increased scrutiny over his government’s past dealings with Qatar, which backed Hamas financially with Israeli approval and has long hosted the group’s political leadership.
Future security strategy
For decades, Israel’s security doctrine has rested on three principles: strong intelligence, deterrence and short wars.
But that changed after October 7.
The government has instead embraced long military campaigns, reflected in the army’s continued presence in “security zones” in Gaza, southern Lebanon and Syria.

It also carries out near-daily operations in the occupied West Bank, has launched two wars with Iran and has conducted strikes against Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi rebels, fuelling debate over the country’s ability to sustain a military deployed on multiple fronts.
Tens of thousands of reservists have been repeatedly mobilised since 2023, often at significant personal and economic cost, while military leaders continue to warn of manpower shortages.

“We have gone from a logic of deterrence and prosperity between wars to a society that lives permanently by the sword,” said Ofer Shelah, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS).

The campaigns have come at a cost to Israel’s reputation, drawing fierce international criticism, particularly over the war in Gaza, where the Palestinian death toll has exceeded 74,000, according to the territory’s health ministry.

Even US President Donald Trump publicly rebuked Netanyahu over Israel’s conduct during the latest conflict with Iran, at one point launching a profanity-laced tirade after fresh Israeli strikes on Lebanon threatened to derail ceasefire negotiations.
Religion, identity, conscription
With the military facing manpower shortages, the debate over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews has evolved into a broader argument over Israel’s identity.

Ultra-Orthodox parties want to preserve exemptions that allow religious students to avoid military service, and they are backed by Netanyahu’s Likud party and, by and large, by its far-right coalition partners.
But opposition parties support ending the exemptions and have said they would refuse to join any government that includes ultra-Orthodox parties.
Eisenkot—who lost a son in the Gaza war—has also taken aim at the exemptions, characterising Netanyahu’s government as one that “promotes evasion of duty without shame”.

Netanyahu, meanwhile, has struggled to strike a balance on the issue, recently criticising the arrest of ultra-Orthodox draft dodgers in an interview, while also insisting that those not engaged in full-time Torah study should enlist.
The issue has spawned protests by ultra-Orthodox demonstrators, including one in which they stormed the home of Israel’s military police chief.
But the divide extends beyond military service.

Just days before parliament was dissolved, the outgoing coalition introduced measures promoting gender separation in some public spaces and passed legislation emphasising the importance of Torah study.
Supporters say these policies strengthen Israel’s Jewish character, but critics argue they move the country toward greater religious influence over public life.
Surging cost of living
While security dominates the political debate, the economy remains a major concern for many voters.
Despite strong economic growth, with GDP more than doubling since 2000 and unemployment historically low, Israelis continue to face one of the world’s highest costs of living.
At the same time, median wages remain below the OECD average, putting increasing pressure on households.
Economists point to long-standing structural problems, including housing shortages, trade barriers and limited competition in key sectors, as the main drivers of high prices.
The wars have added another challenge.
Since 2023, Israel’s defence budget has doubled, placing growing pressure on public finances. — AFP
83b67ce293650c2e: MEXICO CITY, Oct 22 — In a workshop in the Mexican town of San Salvador Huixcolotla, three men use small hammers and chisels to punch holes in thick sheets of tissue paper ahead of the Dia de Muertos (Day of the Dead) festival.
The multicolored paper perforated with intricate folk art designs is known as “papel picado” (pecked paper).
It is a central element in the lavish altars erected to the deceased on November 1-2 and is also used to festoon homes and streets.
Papel picado originated in this small central Mexican town in the late 19th century.
More than a century later, three-quarters of the town’s 17,000 inhabitants are employed in producing the paper, which is exported worldwide.
Despite the advent of AI and 3D printing, many people here continue making the paper by hand.

“We get satisfaction from the idea that our craftsmanship is recognized in other countries and that people see value in handmade things,” Miguel Reynoso, a 58-year-old papel picado producer, told AFP.
Reynoso has been in the business for 40 years.
He and his wife employ over a dozen people, including their four daughters, making decorative banners for clients as far away as South Korea and Japan.
The garlands are in demand year-round for events such as baptisms and “quinceaneras” (girls’ 15th birthdays, a major milestone in Latin America).
But orders skyrocket in the lead-up to the Day of the Dead, when hundreds of thousands of sheets of paper are used to deck out towns and cities.
My tradition
The art of making papel picado was born on ranches outside Huixcolotla.
Following a Mesoamerican tradition, farm workers used to etch simple geometric designs into thick paper made from tree bark.
The arrival of fine tissue paper from China in the mid-19th century revolutionized the process, allowing for greater sophistication.
Nowadays, the paper too is manufactured in Huixcolotla, which prides itself on controlling the entire process.
Even the chisels—straight, curved or zigzag, depending on the motif—are made here.
The palette of colors used in the paper has evolved over time to include shades associated with Mexican design, such as lime and Mexican pink (fuchsia).
Roberto Carlos carefully carves a skull adorned with an elegant hat into a wad of deep purple paper 50 sheets deep.
If the paper tears, he has to discard the lot, which is why you have to “be very delicate,” the 34-year-old artisan explained.
Mari Reynoso, Miguel’s 26-year-old daughter, acknowledged that “industrialization” threatened her town’s bread and butter.
The disappearance of handicrafts, “a symbol of Mexico,” would be a blow to the country’s heritage, she argued.
“Just seeing them makes people say: ‘This is culture, this is my tradition.’” — AFP
156eb47b23d11f0b: SANTIAGO, Oct 22 — The world is hungrier than ever for copper, a key ingredient in green energy and the data centres that power artificial intelligence.
But Chile, which accounts for one-quarter of the world’s supply of the critical mineral, has seen its output of its biggest export fall in recent years.
In August, production fell to its lowest level in 15 years, even though strong global demand is keeping prices buoyant.
Why is output falling?
Chile’s woes are largely due to the age of its mines.
After decades of extraction, the biggest deposits have been depleted, meaning companies have to process ever more ore to obtain the same quantities of the metal.

“You have to invest more money, undertake much greater maintenance efforts, and that also means more demanding technical requirements,” Juan Carlos Guajardo, founder of the Chilean consultancy Plusmining, told AFP.
To offset the drop in productivity, mining companies have moved to expand and modernize their mines.
But several projects suffered delays, cost overruns or technical problems, Nicolas Munoz, an analyst at London-based consultancy CRU Group, noted.
State-owned Codelco was, for example, forced to suspend expansion of the El Teniente mine – Chile’s largest – after studies flagged up seismic risks.
Meanwhile, mines in northern and central Chile were forced to reduce operations in July and August due to heavy rains linked to El Nino that knocked out power and hampered access to the sites.
These setbacks come a year after Codelco’s largest mine, El Teniente, was forced to suspend part of its production for months following an accident that left six workers dead.
How have markets reacted?
The drop in Chile’s output has put pressure on global supplies, causing prices to hit a record US$14,875 (RM60,700) a ton in September.
A further unexpected decline in production could force importers to look for alternative suppliers, according to Munoz.
The International Energy Agency anticipates a 25-per cent copper supply deficit by 2035 if new deposits are not developed worldwide.
Copper’s biggest clients are worried that Chile “does not have a significant production-increase pipeline in sight,” said Guajardo.
“That means the rest of the world will have to make a greater effort (to make up the shortfall).”
Chile’s market share has fallen from 34 per cent in 2010 to around 23 per cent today, according to the US Geological Survey.
The decline is hitting the economy. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz said this month that it had knocked “at least one percentage point” off GDP this year.
How can Chile rebound?
There is no quick fix, according to Guajardo and Munoz, who argue that Chile must restore production at its biggest mines and move forward with expansion and modernization projects.
In the longer term, they say, the country needs to develop new deposits.
“It’s not an issue that can be solved with a law or a regulatory change. It’s a systematic effort that has to be undertaken,” said Guajardo.
Munoz highlights the need to streamline mining permits, attract investment and improve infrastructure, especially in energy, logistics and water, which the industry requires.
CRU consultancy nevertheless forecasts output of around 5.5 million tons of copper in 2027, up from the 5.27 million tons projected by the Chilean Copper Commission for this year.
The medium-term outlook is more positive, with CRU forecasting up to 6 million tons by 2030 as new projects come online. — AFP

ce5b1255ff4fc681: TEHERAN: Anti-American propaganda is a common sight on the streets of the Iranian capital, but authorities have gone a step further with their latest effort – a life-size jail cell with an actor playing US President Donald Trump languishing inside.
The 3D art installation is proving a hit with locals, who have been stopping to take selfies as well as hurl abuse at Trump, who is accused by Teheran of war crimes during the Middle East war.
Since the beginning of the war that began with American and Israeli strikes in February, the Islamic republic has ramped up propaganda operations, with several pieces of artwork going viral.
In their latest campaign, a prison cell is suspended several stories high in Tajrish Square in an upscale neighbourhood of north Teheran.
Inside is an actor dressed in a dark suit and red tie and wearing a prosthetic mask to look like the US president, as he paces around the cell or clutches its bars.
A screen set up nearby shows messages denouncing US "war crimes."
Some locals were having fun with the installation, with one passerby jokingly telling Trump: "Don't worry, we'll pay your bail and get you out!"
Others used it as a target for their anger, with one teenager shouting: "Trump, this time we're going to kill you!"
Teheran's municipal authorities, which are behind the campaign, said they want to remind the capital's residents of Iran's demands for justice.
Iran has portrayed Trump as a war criminal and called for revenge since the conflict began with US-Israeli strikes that killed the country's supreme leader.
Teheran accuses the US president of deliberately targeting civilian sites, including a school and a wedding ceremony, killing dozens of women and children.
Media outlets close to Iranian authorities have said the latest propaganda installation is designed to operate continuously, day and night, seven days a week.--AFP

2949ccf2bc7bf000: KUALA LUMPUR: Ahli Parlimen Machang Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal menggesa kerajaan mempercepat perancangan dan proses membuat keputusan mengenai tenaga nuklear, bagi mengurangkan kebergantungan serta kerentanan Malaysia terhadap kejutan pasaran minyak dan gas global.

Ketika membahaskan Belanjawan 2027 di Dewan Rakyat hari ini, Wan Fayhsal berkata, pergolakan di sekitar Selat Hormuz serta ketidaktentuan global yang semakin meruncing membuktikan keperluan mendesak untuk Malaysia merangka strategi tenaga jangka panjang yang berwibawa.

“Minyak dan gas akan terus jadi cabaran bagi ekonomi kita. Sudah tiba masanya Malaysia mengambil langkah yang serius dan konsisten ke arah usaha membangunkan loji jana kuasa nuklear pertama negara,” katanya.

Wan Fayhsal berkata, sebarang program nuklear pada masa depan menuntut ketegasan dasar serta persediaan jangka panjang, mengambil kira tempoh yang diperlukan untuk mewujudkan kerangka kawal selia, melatih kepakaran, menilai teknologi dan tapak, menjamin pembiayaan, selain membina keyakinan orang ramai.

“(Usaha) membina loji jana kuasa nuklear berskala mega memakan masa yang lama. Ia memerlukan keputusan berani daripada kerajaan serta persediaan rapi jangka panjang,” kata ketua penerangan Wawasan itu.

Beliau menambah, ketiadaan hala tuju yang jelas mengenai tenaga nuklear dalam belanjawan negara dikhuatiri mengekalkan kitaran sama, iaitu krisis global melonjakkan kos bahan api, kerajaan berdepan tekanan hebat untuk terus menampung subsidi petrol dan diesel, manakala kewangan awam akhirnya menanggung beban tersebut.

“Jika alternatif nuklear ini tidak ditangani secara tuntas dalam Belanjawan 2027, saya bimbang kita akan terus ulang skrip serupa, dengan perbelanjaan subsidi bahan api kian melambung sehingga menjejaskan masa depan negara,” katanya.
Beliau menggesa Putrajaya mempercepat reformasi sektor tenaga serta meletakkan keutamaan yang lebih mendesak terhadap perancangan bagi membina loji jana kuasa nuklear pertama negara.

Gesaan itu hadir di tengah-tengah ketidaktentuan berhubung hala tuju tenaga nuklear kerajaan. Rancangan Malaysia Ke-13 (RMK13) menyasarkan penjanaan kuasa nuklear mula beroperasi menjelang 2031, namun Timbalan Perdana Menteri Fadillah Yusof sebelum ini menyatakan keputusan muktamad sama ada menerima pakai tenaga nuklear hanya akan dibuat selepas 2030.
Kerajaan kini sedang meneliti teknologi bersesuaian, potensi lokasi, pembiayaan, kawal selia, kesan alam sekitar, aturan keselamatan, penerimaan awam serta pembangunan kepakaran tempatan.
Putrajaya turut mempertimbangkan reaktor modular kecil, yang bersaiz lebih kompak berbanding loji konvensional dan boleh dibangunkan secara berperingkat.

Wan Fayhsal berkata, isu utama bukanlah tergesa-gesa memulakan pembinaan, sebaliknya memastikan Malaysia tidak menangguhkan keputusan sehingga dihimpit krisis tenaga.

Menurutnya, Malaysia mesti bersedia menghadapi lonjakan permintaan elektrik berikutan percambahan pusat data, kecerdasan buatan (AI), peralihan ke arah elektrifikasi serta sektor pembuatan termaju, di samping mengurangkan pendedahan kepada pasaran bahan api fosil yang tidak menentu.
“Malaysia perlu mempercepat pembaharuan tenaga, diiringi perancangan rapi bagi loji jana kuasa nuklear pertama kita,” katanya.

3a9ed3be591d1fa6: WASHINGTON: The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin announced Thursday a 10-year agreement for the production of 850 F-35 warplanes, underscoring Washington's long-term commitment to the stealth aircraft.
The "framework agreement", which the Pentagon said would "modernise and expand" the F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter programme, still requires congressional approval and funding.

190ebf2a9f95b9a3: TOKYO: Companies and governments worldwide rushed on Thursday to patch critical flaws in the widely used PHP programming language, as a cybersecurity company reported millions of hacking attempts after the vulnerabilities were disclosed.
The push came after governments in Europe and elsewhere took websites offline as a precaution on Wednesday while website operators scrambled to secure systems running the software.

The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki showed how much public and corporate systems rely on the software, and how hard it is to fix such flaws quickly once they are made public.

"It was a long day and a long night, I know for all the IT and security folks ... I've not seen anything like this in a long, long time," Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at a company event in Cologne, Germany, on Thursday.
He said the episode underscored the importance of building digital systems that can be maintained securely.
PHP developers released urgent fixes on Wednesday for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI, urging users to "update immediately".
"Details of these flaws became public before fixes were ready, and attacks have since been reported," said Madeline Lawrence, co-founder of Belgian cybersecurity firm Aikido Security.
"So companies are racing to update against attackers who can use AI to exploit them. That's the whole race," Lawrence said.
As companies and governments deployed patches and suspended websites as a precaution, hacking attempts surged into the millions, according to cloud services firm Cloudflare.
"In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it," Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Wednesday.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now."
From Japan to Finland

Japanese companies, including brokerage Nomura, lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, airline ANA and East Japan Railway said on Thursday they were temporarily suspending some internet services as part of emergency measures.
Insurer Tokio Marine Holdings said it had suspended the website of a group company.
Japan's finance ministry and meteorological agency partially suspended online services to implement safety measures, while Japan's National Tax Agency temporarily took down its service.

The precautionary shutdowns underscore growing concerns over cybersecurity in Japan, which recorded more cyber incidents in the first nine months of the year than in all of last year, according to data from TrendAI.
French telecoms group Orange said it had temporarily suspended access to certain PHP-based websites and applications across several subsidiaries as a precaution.
Tencent Cloud, one of China's largest cloud-computing providers, urged customers to install updated PHP versions but stopped short of calling for widespread website shutdowns.

Finland's state IT services provider Valtori said it had continued installing PHP security patches overnight and was gradually lifting precautionary service blocks after shutting down government public web services a day earlier.
"Restoring services can take days or even weeks, as in addition to updates, the systems need to be carefully tested," Valtori Director General Hannu Naumanen said in a statement.
Valtori said the outages were not caused by exploitation of the vulnerabilities or by a cyber breach, and that it was not aware of any active exploitation of the flaws.
Several Asian governments ordered cybersecurity inspections related to the PHP vulnerabilities on Thursday.
China's industry ministry urged organisations and users to inspect systems immediately and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP.
It also recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring and changing accounts, passwords and keys where necessary.
South Korea raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures, citing concerns over an increased risk of hacking attacks.

Youth clubs were left unpaid after JDT failed to complete the vetting within required deadlines.

"The Committee recalled in this respect that said levy functions as a substitute for interest on late payment, as the Respondent's first failure of the compliance assessment prevents the training clubs from receiving their training rewards in a timely fashion," the document said.

aa6ca27ad5d08b45: TAIPEI: A powerful typhoon headed towards Taiwan on Thursday, triggering the cancellation of dozens of flights and prompting warnings for locals to prepare for heavy rain, strong winds and giant waves.
Typhoon Champi is expected to sweep past Taiwan's northeast coast on Friday and Saturday as it moves towards China and Japan, Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA) said.
Champi has maximum sustained wind speeds of nearly 195km per hour, according to the latest update from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.
It was previously classed as a super typhoon, with reported maximum speeds of nearly 300kph, but has since weakened.
"Everyone is urged to remain vigilant and be prepared for the strong winds and heavy rains brought by the typhoon," Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te said in a Facebook post.
Champi is the latest in a busy Pacific storm season turbo-charged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming in the equatorial Pacific.
The storm is expected to dump up to 900mm of rain in the mountainous regions of northern and northeastern Taiwan from Thursday to Saturday, and whip up waves more than six metres tall.
Work and classes on Friday have been cancelled in many cities and counties across the island.
More than 23,000 military personnel are on standby to help with rescue efforts. Over 150 domestic and international flights were cancelled for Thursday ahead of the storm.
"Typhoon Champi is expected to have its most significant impact starting all day tomorrow through the first half of Saturday," CWA forecaster Jason Cheng told AFP.
"Currently, the typhoon has a storm radius of 320km... Compared to the previous Typhoon Bavi, Champi's storm area is not as vast," Cheng said.
Millions of people in eastern China also prepared for torrential downpours and flash flooding in the coming days.
China's Ministry of Water Resources initiated a level-four emergency response on Thursday for flooding in Shanghai and the coastal provinces of Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Fujian.
Level four is the lowest in China's emergency response hierarchy.

The ministry warned that Champi could bring "a period of significant rainfall" from Friday to Sunday, with "heavy to torrential downpours" expected in some areas, including "most of Shanghai and eastern Zhejiang."
Japan's two major airlines cancelled more than 110 flights from Thursday to Saturday.
The United Nations said Wednesday that the El Nino system gripping the planet is heading off the charts, and that countries should take urgent action to prepare for the worst.
El Nino is expected to peak in December, but the human impact is set to last into 2027 and beyond.

The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate human-caused global warming.--AFP

7fdb75d069c99610: KUALA LUMPUR: Putrajaya should consider granting Langkawi more fiscal autonomy to manage its taxes and use the revenue for local development, says Suhaimi Abdullah (PN-Langkawi).

He said that while the island had generated billions of ringgit from tourism, a large portion of the tax revenue went into federal coffers, although various levels of government had to bear development and service costs.

Suhaimi suggested a decentralised “Langkawi Fiscal Autonomy Model” based on arrangements in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China, or in Switzerland where each of the 26 cantons enjoys a high degree of tax autonomy.
“Under this model, Langkawi would collect its own taxes, retain a large portion of the revenue and be responsible for significant spending.

"Meanwhile, the government can still handle federal matters such as defence, national security, immigration, foreign policy and some strategic infrastructure,” said the MP when debating the 2027 budget in the Dewan Rakyat.
Suhaimi said Langkawi could be empowered to manage local council and land taxes, as well as licences, and introduce levies on tourism, hotels and ferries.
He said that with more than 3.2 million visitors recorded in 2025, a moderate levy of RM30 per person could generate nearly RM100 million a year.

“Combined with existing revenue and other tourism-related sources, Langkawi could manage around RM250 million to RM350 million a year to finance sanitation, transport, water supply and tourism development without waiting for federal allocations.”
Separately, Suhaimi said small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in Langkawi were calling for a review of the taxes imposed on their products when shipped to the mainland.
He said SME-produced goods such as handicrafts and snacks became more expensive when sold on the mainland because of these taxes.

“Snacks become expensive when sold in Kuala Perlis, even though flour prices on the mainland and the island are the same. Therefore, SMEs are asking for a review of taxes on goods made in Langkawi,” he said.

d3061e13f4e86a99: HONG KONG: China Evergrande Group's liquidators have recovered US$435.9 million from asset sales and loan recoveries so far, highlighting the challenge of repaying creditors with claims of about US$46 billion against the developer.

In their second progress report since a Hong Kong court ordered Evergrande's liquidation in January 2024, the liquidators, Edward Middleton and Tiffany Wong of Alvarez & Marsal, said on Thursday they aimed to make a first interim dividend payment to creditors in the first half of 2027, although the amount has yet to be determined.

Evergrande, once China's top property developer, defaulted on most of its roughly US$300 billion in liabilities and became a symbol of the property crisis that has weighed on the world's second-largest economy.
The liquidators said they had raised the US$435.9 million through the sale of assets including aircraft, artwork and club memberships, as well as the settlement of loan receivables.

They said 96 of the 107 artworks found at Evergrande's Hong Kong headquarters had been sold for US$28.8 million at a loss. The collection included works by Picasso, Monet and Warhol, as well as sculptures by Moore and Hepworth.

Other assets being sold include a private jet expected to fetch about US$12 million in the fourth quarter. The liquidators are also seeking a US$2 million refund from a US university for part of a donation made in 2020.

The liquidators have taken control of more than 100 Evergrande subsidiaries across multiple jurisdictions, but said prospects for recovering assets held by mainland Chinese subsidiaries were "considered remote."
In August, Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan, 67, was sentenced to life imprisonment by a Chinese court, which also ordered the confiscation of his personal assets.
Industry experts say Evergrande's liquidation could take more than a decade to complete given the scale and complexity of the group.--REUTERS
87b63b9756c278ab: PARIS: French authorities on Thursday imposed bans or restrictions on fresh protests springing up in the wake of demonstrations last weekend that degenerated into the worst street violence in years.

President Emmanuel Macron said, after chairing a meeting of key ministers and intelligence officials, that curfews and other security measures would be imposed, including bans on "groups without legitimacy" holding protests.

"The priority is a return to calm," he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide "the next steps" for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.

Officials are still reeling from the clashes, widespread looting and vandalism of public buildings that broke out on Oct 17, on the margins of mass demonstrations of more than half a million people against the surging cost of living.

Macron's government has admitted police lost control, and candidates jockeying to succeed him in presidential elections in six months' time argue that authorities are incapable or unwilling to calm the situation.
The worst of the violence, Macron said, "was led by organised ultra-left groups aiming to bring down the republic".
Protests banned
A Paris protest Thursday organised by students – who had held four weeks of protests before the Oct 17 rallies – was banned by the capital's police.
"The authorities are trying to make a distinction between 'good' and 'bad' protesters," said a university student leader, Coppelia Moreau, as lawyers requested a court injunction against the ban.
"What we are seeing is a government that doesn't want any demonstrations at all. That goes against the right to demonstrate," she told journalists.
Authorities on Thursday also declared a ban on "all protests" in the southwestern city of Lyon on Saturday.
France's third-biggest city suffered the looting of 200 to 300 shops last weekend and the torching of a tourist office in what its mayor described as hours of "chaos".
Other cities, including Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon, issued bans on protests in their city centres.

In Paris, the city's police said Thursday that the march planned for Saturday could be held in the east of the capital, starting at Bastille, but was banned from heading into the city centre, where shops and major public buildings are located.
The Yellow Vest movement organising the cost-of-living rallies along with unions said it did not agree with the order.
"We won't sign off on it," said Benjamin Ball, who runs an online map showing the planned locations of Saturday's demonstrations.
Detentions and dialogue
The French government has been projecting a firm response in the wake of last weekend's violence, although Macron has said he would not go as far as to call a state of emergency.
Justice minister Gerald Darmanin said Wednesday that 174 people of the 2,500 arrested since last weekend had been locked up, and more than 900 were being prosecuted.
On Thursday, a 66-year-old man was arrested over the arson last weekend of the 19th-century town hall of Limoges, prosecutors said. A man in his 30s was already arrested Tuesday over the same crime.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader whom voter surveys place as the frontrunner candidate ahead of the April-May presidential elections, has accused Macron and his centrist government of being too soft and lacking authority.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, a far-left candidate criticised by the government for not condemning the protest violence, blamed authorities' "non-stop brutal repression" for the unrest.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Thursday was to host a meeting of top officials from France's main parties to hear their grievances and seek cooperation. While most were sending their leaders, Le Pen's National Rally was to be represented by a lower-ranking party official.
Lecornu was to follow that up with another meeting with mayors, and on Monday he will meet student groups.
6e8cff97380e5917: PETALING JAYA: A Porsche Cayenne driver was sentenced to five days in prison and fined RM10,000 by the magistrates' court here after pleading guilty to dangerous driving of the luxury car on a highway near Bandar Kinrara.

How far can we push computing?

On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued. We simply had not built the tools yet.

He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size. But that easy descent has now stalled. Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance.
Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement.
Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing.
—Volkan Gurses

Scott Shambaugh didn’t think twice when he denied an AI agent’s request to contribute to matplotlib, a software library he helps manage. Then things got weird.

In the middle of the night, Shambaugh opened his email to discover the agent had retaliated with a blog post. Titled “Gatekeeping in Open Source: The Scott Shambaugh Story,” the post accused him of rejecting the code out of a fear of being supplanted by AI. “He tried to protect his little fiefdom,” the agent wrote. “It’s insecurity, plain and simple.”
Shambaugh isn’t alone in facing misbehaving agents—and they’re unlikely to stop at harassment. Read the full story.
—Grace Huckins

f3d6ca5d7070da35: MOSCOW: Russia has deepened a crackdown on European companies in response to Europe's support for Ukraine, while largely sparing US firms as Moscow courts business ties with Washington, Russian officials and US business people said.

Of 20 foreign-owned firms that Russian president Vladimir Putin has placed under temporary administration since Donald Trump's inauguration as US president in January 2025, only three were linked to the US, with the remainder controlled by European companies, a Reuters analysis of official data shows.

A person close to Russian financial regulators said that while business negotiations were underway with Washington, it was not in Moscow's interest to take as tough a line on US firms as the Kremlin was adopting towards those from Europe.

US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday for talks aimed at resolving the war in Ukraine. Russian news agencies reported Putin told Witkoff he was interested in restoring economic ties with the US.

Ukraine and its allies have voiced concerns that the US is backing away from Kyiv, and Trump has criticised Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries even as European leaders have lined up behind Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy.

Russia, citing Europe's wartime support for Ukraine and involvement in "direct battlefield hostilities", has since last month taken control of local units of Swiss food group Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro.
Last week it seized control of the local assets of four smaller companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium.

"Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in "illegal expropriations of Russian property".
Nestle, which said in September it would take steps to protect its rights in Russia, declined to comment further. The other companies did not respond to requests for comment.
A spokesman for Switzerland's state secretariat for economic affairs said that the available information supported the perception that more European than US firms were being hit.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Commenting on the report after its publication, the Kremlin said that US companies were better treated than their European rivals because of Trump's efforts to achieve peace in Ukraine.

"The American administration is doing a lot to help bring about a peaceful settlement; the European capitals are doing nothing to help while doing a lot to prolong the military action," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
'We have Trump"
Russia's relations with the Trump administration, meanwhile, have warmed.
The US announced a deal this month to buy Russian diesel, and other deals, including on gas, have been discussed at meetings in recent months.
Trump signed an executive order on Saturday waiving key sanctions and tariffs on Russian goods.

Russian negotiator Kirill Dmitriev, a US-educated investment banker who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and has pushed in talks for the return and expansion of US firms, hailed the move as a "historic moment".

Trump's envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner have used the prospect of multibillion-dollar deals with Russia as an incentive to push Putin toward a peaceful settlement since the start of talks in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, in February 2025.
Dmitriev said last week Russia and the US would soon announce new joint initiatives that could move ahead before the war ends.
The US has previously signalled that deals are unlikely while the conflict continues.
One person familiar with the situation said that some Russian officials who do not support peace efforts could yet push for the Kremlin's actions to include more US companies.
The RDIF's only current partnership with a US company is a joint investment with New York-listed Titan International in a tyre factory in Volgograd.
Another person familiar with the situation said Dmitriev has in private highlighted this as an example of a thriving US business in Russia.
Titan did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump's commitment to economic cooperation with Russia and ongoing talks have helped to protect the interests of US companies, two US business people in Moscow said.

American Chamber of Commerce Russia President Robert Agee said in December last year that European firms in Russia were less optimistic than American ones, citing European policy. The chamber estimates there are some 300 US firms left in Russia.
"We have Trump and they don't, and our hopes are linked to him," Agee told Russian media last year. Agee and the chamber declined to comment further for this story.

Russia did target some mid-sized US firms during its property redistribution drive after the start of the war. One report estimated Moscow seized more than US$50 billion worth of private property from both Russian and foreign owners.

The European Commission in Brussels declined to comment on the number of EU firms being targeted relative to US ones, but said the recent asset seizures were without due process and amounted to "forced expropriation in all but name".
"This follows a clear pattern of economic retaliation," a Commission spokesman told Reuters, adding that the moves showed that "Russia is not a safe environment for business".
"The EU has measures in place to respond. We can sanction those profiting from forced expropriations," they added.
1d0ef88ed0aec060: MERCEDES-Benz Malaysia has invested RM2.2 million in a specialised service hub for the Mercedes-AMG One hypercar, making the nation the only location in Southeast Asia equipped to service the Formula 1-derived model.
Located at Hap Seng Star's Bukit Tinggi facility, the hub joins a limited global network serving owners of the road-legal hypercar, of which only 275 units were produced worldwide.
The facility will support owners across Southeast Asia, complementing an existing service hub in Japan.
It is equipped with specialised high-voltage tools, vehicle-specific diagnostic systems and controlled storage and working conditions to meet the model's technical requirements.
The Malaysia-based technicians have undergone specialised training and received Mercedes-AMG certification to carry out approved diagnostic, maintenance and servicing procedures.
The team will also coordinate directly with Mercedes-AMG specialists in Affalterbach, Germany for technical support.
The Mercedes-AMG One combines a 1.6-litre V6 turbocharged engine with four electric motors, producing a total system output of more than 1,063 horsepower.
Its hybrid powertrain draws directly on F1 technology, making servicing more complex than that of conventional performance cars.
Mercedes-Benz Malaysia chief executive officer Martin Schulz said the facility builds on Malaysia's existing role in supporting the company's regional operations.

The hub's location also provides access to Mercedes-Benz Parts Logistics Asia Pacific's operations in Malaysia, which the company said would help streamline parts distribution and reduce delays in maintenance and repairs.
Other services include regional technical support, dedicated liaison officers for international customers and digital systems for diagnostic reporting and service updates.
The investment comes as Malaysia seeks to expand its high-value services sector under the 13th Malaysia Plan for 2026 to 2030.
The facility adds a specialised automotive service capability to the country's existing logistics and aftersales operations.
Hap Seng Star, which operates the Bukit Tinggi facility, will provide servicing for AMG One owners from Malaysia and other regional markets.
af357d922c7912d9: KUALA LUMPUR: The High Court's decision to stay Perikatan Nasional's suspension and deregistration has strengthened the coalition's resolve ahead of the Melaka election.

"Today's positive decision will further strengthen PN's resolve to consolidate its position, offer the people the best policies and services, and translate these efforts into public support in the upcoming Melaka election," he said in a statement.

"Today's decision is in line with the late Sultan Azlan Shah's judgment in the 1979 case of Director of Lands and Mines, Federal Territory v Sri Lempah Enterprise Sdn Bhd, which stated that 'every power must have legal limits, otherwise it will lead to dictatorial rule'," he said.

e5c6f83624ef50bc: YEREVAN: Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an "extremely high risk" of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned Thursday.
In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96% of the planet's coral reef systems as "critically endangered" – its highest risk category.
Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world's oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.

"The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

"Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events," said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean (CORDIO) East Africa, a conservation organisation.
For their assessment, researchers used the "middle-of-the-road" scenario from the UN's panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7°C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
The world is on track for 2.6°C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the UN warned Wednesday.
"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said in a statement.
Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators help control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said.
The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63 percent of coral reef ecosystems.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats.
Critically endangered coral
The IUCN's analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.

The world's largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered – Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in Southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean's Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs.
A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals – which build its living foundation – largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges.

The report was released during the UN's COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, where governments are under pressure to make progress on a landmark pact to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world "are not yet lost".

If scientists look only at what has happened over the past 50 years, excluding future climate projections, 24% of coral reef ecosystems would be deemed critically endangered instead of 96%, the IUCN said.
"It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming," said IUCN director general Grethel Aguilar.

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them."

A study published in the journal Nature last week found that, by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at "elevated relative risk of extinction", with climate change the main driver of this decline.
4b0be0281398854a: KUALA LUMPUR: Wawasan information chief and Machang MP Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal has urged Putrajaya to accelerate planning and decision-making on nuclear energy to reduce Malaysia’s vulnerability to external oil and gas shocks.

Debating the 2027 budget in the Dewan Rakyat today, Wan Fayhsal said the situation around the Strait of Hormuz and wider global instability showed why Malaysia needed to develop a credible long-term energy strategy.
“Oil and gas will remain a major challenge to our economy. It is time for Malaysia to take serious and consistent steps towards developing our first nuclear power plant.”

Wan Fayhsal said any future nuclear programme would require a bold policy decision and long-term preparation, given the time needed to establish the regulatory framework, develop expertise, assess technologies and sites, secure financing, and build public confidence.
“Building a mega nuclear power plant takes a long time. It requires a courageous decision by the government and sufficient long-term preparation.”

Wan Fayhsal said the absence of a clear direction on nuclear energy in the national budget risked perpetuating the same cycle: global disruptions driving up fuel costs, the government facing mounting pressure to subsidise petrol and diesel, and public finances bearing the consequences.

“If the nuclear alternative is not addressed clearly in the 2027 budget, I worry that we will repeat the same script, with fuel subsidies becoming increasingly bloated and leaving a hole in the country’s future.”
He called on Putrajaya to accelerate energy reforms and give greater urgency to the planning needed for the first nuclear plant.

The call comes amid uncertainty over the government’s nuclear energy plans. The 13th Malaysia Plan envisions nuclear power generation commencing operations by 2031 but deputy prime minister Fadillah Yusof had said a final decision on whether to adopt nuclear energy would only be made after 2030.

The government is presently studying the appropriate technology, potential locations, financing, regulations, environmental impact, safety arrangements, public acceptance and development of local expertise.

It is also considering small modular reactors, which are not as large as conventional nuclear plants and may be deployed in stages. No decision has been made on the technology, capacity or location of any future facility.
Wan Fayhsal said the issue was not about rushing into construction but ensuring Malaysia does not defer the decision until after it has been overtaken by an energy crisis.

He said Malaysia must prepare for rising electricity demand from data centres, artificial intelligence, electrification and advanced manufacturing, while reducing its exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets.
“Malaysia must accelerate energy reform, with careful planning for our first nuclear power plant.”
96554623e811c4a7: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Police have crippled ‘Geng Yunaa’, believed to be involved in 17 cases of child prostitution and trafficking for sexual exploitation, following ‘Ops Angel’ in the Klang Valley from Sept 24 to 26.

Bukit Aman Criminal Investigation Department director Datuk M. Kumar said seven individuals, aged between 18 and 44, were detained under the Security Offences (Special Measures) Act 2012 (SOSMA) until tomorrow.
He said two other group members were already being held at Kajang Prison and Henry Gurney School in Melaka for offences related to child trafficking and prostitution.

“The group carried out sexual exploitation through prostitution by recruiting local teenagers, foreign nationals and underage children, who were exploited and made victims of prostitution in Selangor and Kuala Lumpur.
“To attract customers, the group used the Telegram application to promote prostitution services, with an estimated 20 to 30 sex workers operating daily,” he said in a statement today.

Kumar said customers were charged between RM200 and RM350, depending on the package and service location. Payments were believed to have been made in cash or through Touch ‘n Go or banking QR codes to prostitution agents linked to the group.
He said the group was believed to have served about 100 customers daily, collecting RM150 from each customer, while the remainder was paid to the individuals being exploited.
Based on these estimates, the group could generate RM15,000 a day, or RM450,000 a month, equivalent to RM5.4 million a year if the activity continued at the same rate.
“This activity is deeply concerning because it not only involves trafficking in human beings for profit but also exploits children, who should be protected from abuse and sexual exploitation.
“More worryingly, the sexual exploitation of underage children can leave long-lasting psychological trauma, damage their emotional, moral and social development, and affect their future,” he said.
Kumar said Geng Yunaa, which had been active since early 2024, comprised 10 members aged between 18 and 44 and was led by a 30-year-old local man.
During the operation, police also seized various items believed to be linked to prostitution activities, including 14 mobile phones, six boxes of contraceptive medication, towels and lubricating gel.
“Checks found that several of those arrested had previous records for various offences, including prostitution, human trafficking, drug distribution and fraud.
“We have also identified another group member who remains at large, and efforts to track down the suspect are ongoing,” he said.

Kumar said the investigation papers had been referred to the Serious Crimes Unit of the Attorney-General’s Chambers, which had agreed that nine members of the group be charged under Section 130V(1) of the Penal Code at the Petaling Jaya Sessions Court tomorrow. — Bernama
3fab4dbe9471d850: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — National swimmers Abd Halim Mohammad and Shahafiq Abdullah rose to the occasion at the Asian Para Games today, delivering a silver and a bronze medal respectively to take Malaysia’s medal haul in the pool to four.
