2711930215c9377d: HONG KONG: Malaysian actress Jacquelin Ch'ng has opened up about the reasons behind her divorce from Taiwanese businessman Brian Yang, revealing that several promises made before their marriage were never kept.
In a recent web show, the 46-year-old said they had agreed on living arrangements and how often they would see each other before tying the knot in March 2020.
"I naturally believed that those promises would be kept, but many problems arose after we got married, and some of those promises were never fulfilled," she said.
The former couple divorced in November 2022.
The TVB star explained that divorce proceedings in Hong Kong typically take about a year to finalise.
"The paperwork was settled in early 2023, so we were technically married for only a year.
"That same year, we were also dealing with the Covid-19 pandemic and could not travel by plane. When you add everything up, we probably spent only a few months together," she noted.
Ch'ng added that they actually understood each other better while dating than after tying the knot.
"After getting married, we actually did not know each other that well," she said.
Despite the split, Ch'ng remains on good terms with Yang, who even congratulated her on her marriage to Hong Kong senior police inspector Matthew Wong on Oct 8 last year.
When asked about her views on marriage certificates, the actress stressed that a piece of paper cannot guarantee a lasting relationship, adding that a partner's personality is far more important.
She previously revealed that she did not sign a marriage certificate with Wong, saying she did not consider it necessary.
Ch'ng, who is the daughter of the late Malaysian tycoon Datuk Bill Ch'ng, also addressed rumours that she is worth HK$800 million (RM416 million).
While acknowledging that she comes from a well-to-do family, she laughed off the reported fortune as completely untrue.
"If I had that kind of money, I would not be working! I would be travelling the world," she quipped.
84989ca3edb9b386: BANGKOK: Thailand plans to tighten cannabis regulations and propose tougher penalties for violations as part of broader efforts to strengthen drug prevention and enforcement.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said the proposed amendments to the Narcotics Act concerning cannabis were discussed at the third meeting of the Office of the Narcotics Control Board (ONCB) this year on Thursday.
"Drug policies must be guided by scientific evidence, facts and the public interest," he said in a statement published on the Royal Thai Government website.
He said the government would maintain a clear distinction between medical cannabis use and recreational consumption.

The Ministry of Public Health and relevant agencies had also been directed to inspect licensed establishments and take legal action against operators who breach their licence conditions, including possible revocation, he said.

Anutin said the meeting also discussed amendments to drug laws to improve enforcement against drug possession, including small-quantity offences, while ensuring that treatment and rehabilitation were appropriately considered alongside legal action.

Anutin said he had also instructed the Customs Department to step up inspections, intelligence gathering and random checks to prevent the illegal export of goods, particularly those potentially linked to narcotics.

"Exports of cannabis stems, leaves and flower buds must strictly comply with Thai law, while cannabidiol (CBD) extracts could be exported subject to licensing requirements and regulations set by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)," he said.
Thailand decriminalised cannabis in 2022, but amid concerns about recreational use and the rapid expansion of cannabis-related businesses, the government has since moved to tighten regulations.
On Sept 22, the Thai cabinet approved a draft Cannabis and Hemp Act to restrict cannabis strictly to medical use and phase out the recreational market.

Separately, on security in Thailand's southern border provinces, Anutin said the National Security Council had convened relevant security, intelligence and administrative agencies to formulate a unified operational strategy.
"The aim is to ensure that all agencies have a common understanding and work together under the same strategic plan in a unified manner," he said.

He added that security agencies had been instructed to closely monitor developments, strengthen surveillance and coordinate intelligence to prevent further escalation and safeguard public order and residents' safety. — BERNAMA
2ca878bda9e7802e: PETALING JAYA: Peningkatan peruntukan persekutuan buat Sabah dan Sarawak mesti diterjemahkan kepada pembangunan yang benar-benar dirasai rakyat, kata Menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri (Hal Ehwal Sabah dan Sarawak) Mustapha Sakmud.
Beliau berkata, kerajaan tidak boleh sekadar berpuas hati mengumumkan peruntukan berbilion ringgit jika masalah infrastruktur di kedua-dua negeri masih berlarutan.
“Kita tidak boleh berpuas hati dengan pengumuman berbilion ringgit jika hasilnya belum benar-benar dirasai rakyat.
“Saya amat memahami kehendak rakyat yang masih berdepan masalah jalan raya, bekalan air, elektrik dan kelewatan projek infrastruktur termasuk Lebuhraya Pan Borneo.
“Peningkatan peruntukan mesti diterjemahkan kepada pelaksanaan yang lebih pantas dan berkesan,” katanya menerusi hantaran Facebook.
Menurutnya, peruntukan persekutuan bagi Sabah meningkat daripada RM13 bilion pada 2022 kepada RM17.2 bilion tahun lalu, manakala peruntukan bagi tahun ini berjumlah RM17.6 bilion.
Bagi Sarawak, jumlah itu meningkat daripada RM10.2 bilion pada 2022 kepada RM15.4 bilion pada 2025, dengan RM15.1 bilion diperuntukkan tahun ini, tambahnya.

Sementara itu, Mustapha mempertahankan rekod kerajaan Madani dalam melaksanakan Perjanjian Malaysia 1963 (MA63) dengan berkata, 12 daripada 16 perkara yang telah diselesaikan dicapai di bawah pentadbiran semasa, termasuk pemberian khas interim Sabah yang meningkat kepada RM1.5 bilion tahun ini daripada RM600 juta tahun lepas.
Bagaimanapun, Mustapha menegaskan pemberian interim itu bukan penyelesaian muktamad bagi tuntutan Sabah terhadap 40% hasil bersih persekutuan yang diperoleh dari negeri itu.
Rundingan mengenai mekanisme, jumlah dan garis masa pembayaran masih diteruskan antara kerajaan persekutuan dengan kerajaan negeri, katanya.
0c2711a6a9afe475: STRASBOURG: Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court (ICC) was on Thursday awarded the European Union's top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump.

"The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice," said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize "at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges".

"Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law," ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
This month, the US announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Trump's administration has vowed to dismantle the court "brick by brick", furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.

The win comes after ex-ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as UN rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this month -- a choice Trump slammed as "disgraceful", arguing the award should have gone to him.

The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions -- which will come into force in six months -- and has said it is "ready to take any necessary measures" to make sure the court can keep working.
Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government.
The nominees are put forward by the political groupings in the EU and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December.

faef03d2a7708749: PETALING JAYA: The federal territories Islamic religious department (Jawi) and 22 others have asked the Court of Appeal to overturn a ruling ordering them to pay lawyer and activist Siti Kasim RM160,000 for her wrongful arrest and detention in 2016.

Berita Harian reported that senior federal counsel Ng Siew Wee, representing Jawi, 15 of its officers and seven others, told the court that the officers were only trying to enforce a religious ruling, or fatwa.
She said even if the officers had misunderstood the law, an honest mistake should not automatically be treated as an abuse of power.
“An honest mistake about the law is not misconduct in public office,” she said.
Ng also said there was no evidence that the Jawi officers who lodged a police report against Siti had acted dishonestly to have her charged with obstructing a public servant.
She argued that the High Court judge had erred in assessing witness testimony and relying on evidence from an earlier criminal case.
However, Siti's lawyer, A Saha Deva, said the officers went ahead with the raid without checking whether they had the legal authority to do so.
“They did not care whether they had the authority or not. They went ahead with the raid anyway,” he said.
Saha Deva said the High Court had properly considered the evidence and applied the law in finding the officers had misused their powers.

The case dates back to April 3, 2016, when Siti was arrested during a Jawi raid on a private fundraising dinner. She was taken to the Dang Wangi police headquarters and held for about four hours before being released.

She was later charged with obstructing a Jawi officer from carrying out official duties, but was acquitted by the magistrates’ court in August 2020 after the prosecution failed to establish a case against her.

Siti filed a civil suit against Jawi and the government in September 2019, claiming compensation for wrongful arrest and illegal detention, saying she had only been carrying out her duties as a lawyer during the raid.
On July 18 last year, the High Court ruled in her favour and awarded her RM160,000 in damages and RM100,000 in legal costs.

The three-member Court of Appeal bench chaired by Justice Noorin Badaruddin, sitting with Justices Shahnaz Sulaiman and Meor Hashimi Abdul Hamid, fixed Nov 5 for case management to determine the date of its decision.

23ccaa33fc8aa297: SURABAYA: Indonesian schoolchildren prayed for rain on Thursday as another firefighter lost his life battling drought-fuelled blazes consuming forests and peatlands and blanketing parts of Southeast Asia in a sickening haze.
Wildfires have burned more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas – a figure the government has not confirmed or denied.
The resulting haze has sickened hundreds of thousands in Indonesia and reached as far as Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.

In East Java, where fires have ravaged several regencies and conservation areas including Mount Bromo and the Baluran National Park, the governor urged communities to come together to "pray for rain."

"Many areas are experiencing drought, including fires and so on... Religion offers a way to solve the problem of drought," teacher Mohamad Jatim told AFP of prayers organised at his school in Surabaya, the capital of East Java.
"As people of faith, we are of course optimistic."
In Malang, also in the province, some 250 pupils bowed in prayer with their teachers at a vocational high school.
"We hope that this... will bring rain soon," said headmaster Lusia Andriani.
"There have... been many cases of acute respiratory infections in Indonesia, partly because the rain has not fallen for a prolonged period."
- FIREFIGHTER KILLED -
Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year's blazes have been particularly severe, making hundreds of thousands of people ill.
The haze has prompted school closures in Malaysia and East Timor, and has drifted into Singapore and as far afield as the Philippines.
Five firefighters died in East Java last week after they were overwhelmed by smoke and flames in the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park.
Another firefighter died on Wednesday in South Kalimantan on Indonesia's part of Borneo island.
The Mahatir Mohammad Zain Foundation, a disaster relief NGO, said the 51-year-old volunteer passed away after falling ill with chest tightness while helping fight a fire in the Barito Kuala Regency.
His death was "a reminder of the risks volunteers face in handling forest and land fires", said the foundation.
The crisis has sparked protests against the government's perceived slow response, as well as a court case against President Prabowo Subianto and other officials in West Kalimantan.

In the capital Jakarta, a dozen demonstrators gathered outside the Chinese embassy on Thursday demanding importers of Indonesian palm oil, mining and forestry products stand in "solidarity" with Indonesia.
Back in Malang, resident Ahmad Saifuddin joined others in praying for divine intervention.
"For the past few days, I have been wondering why almost everyone is trying to solve these disasters using logic. Why don't we try seeking a solution from the heavens instead?" he told AFP.--AFP

93b4e3302ce543c2: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday.

92172c6cdd54f51a: BERLIN: AI chip giant Nvidia's boss Jensen Huang said on Thursday that warnings AI could wipe out humanity were "cheap" attempts to grab headlines.

While such statements generate "headlines", they were "made up" and "cheap", added Huang, whose visit to Berlin is the final stop of a European tour.
After incidents of the technology getting around controls during tests, there has been a heated debate about whether AI presents an existential risk to humanity.

In September, a researcher resigned from Anthropic with a stark warning that leading AI labs were "gambling with our lives", and the bosses of Anthropic and fellow industry giant OpenAI have called for a slowdown.

ff1084399d13e63e: MANCHESTER, Oct 22 — Enzo Maresca said it is his job as Manchester City boss to help Phil Foden rediscover his best form after the England international ended his long goal drought.
Foden had not scored for 10 months before netting in City’s 3-2 win over Ipswich last weekend and then scored a Champions League hat-trick in a 5-1 rout of AEK Athens on Tuesday.
The 26-year-old swept the board of personal awards for the Premier League’s best player in the 2023/24 season after a 27-goal campaign.
But Foden, who has admitted struggling with mental health issues, has failed to hit top form for the past two seasons.

“Since we started I sat down with Phil two or three times, especially at the beginning. Just to show him, I don’t know if love is the right word to use, but just to show him how important he is,” said Maresca, who took charge of City in June.
“I said many times that I know Phil from years ago so I know how for different reasons, the last few years it was not good enough.
“When you have more players like Phil available, you are a better team because again it’s a matter of improving players. If you improve the players, you improve the team.
“So for me, I think it’s my duty to try to help Phil to be again one of the best players in England.”
Other than a 4-2 Champions League defeat to holders Paris Saint-Germain, Maresca has made a flawless start to the daunting task of succeeding Pep Guardiola at the Etihad Stadium.
The Italian is the first manager ever to win his first seven Premier League games in charge of a new club.
However, City’s fine form has been overshadowed by the threat of severe sanctions against the club for widespread flouting of Premier League financial rules.
A large points deduction, which could lead to relegation, is likely unless City win an appeal against a guilty verdict on more than 100 charges of wrongdoing.
Maresca said the mood in the dressing room remained buoyant despite the cloud hanging over the club.
“In any club, when you lose important players, many important players, and you lose the manager after 10 years, it always takes time to compete again,” he said on Thursday.
“But this organisation last summer changed many important players, changed the manager after 10 years and we are competing at the moment.”
City travel to Aston Villa on Saturday, boosted by the return of Erling Haaland.
The Norwegian, who has scored 12 times in nine appearances this season, missed the AEK Athens match after picking up a foot injury against Ipswich.
Matheus Nunes, Mateo Kovacic and Nico O’Reilly remain injury doubts. — AFP
f591f88e8ecd619f: KYIV: Moscow firing ballistic missiles at Ukraine shortly after talks between US envoy Steve Witkoff and Russia's Vladimir Putin showed the Kremlin's position on the war had not changed, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday.

The Kremlin had said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month, though dismissed new ideas brought by Witkoff -- developed with European countries and Ukraine -- as lacking substance.
Russia hit a dozen Ukrainian regions overnight, including Kyiv, killing at least two people and wounding 34, Zelensky said, adding that children were among those hurt.
Residential houses, energy sites, a shopping mall and a monastery had been damaged in Kyiv, where Russia has significantly intensified its strikes ahead of winter.
Zelensky said the latest strikes began "almost immediately" after US President Donald Trump's envoy Witkoff held hours-long talks with Putin in Saint Petersburg.
Russia also said it had downed 808 Ukrainian drones fired overnight and that two people were wounded in Moscow.
Witkoff faced widespread criticism for calling Putin a "humanitarian" after Moscow released an elderly US citizen who had been jailed on charges of fighting for Ukraine as a "mercenary".
Trump sought an optimistic tone as his envoy returned from Russia, saying Wednesday that negotiators were "maybe now the closest we've been" to ending the war.
But in Kyiv and European capitals, hopes for a breakthrough were slim, with many worried the White House was siding with Moscow.
"Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian 'humanitarians' since yesterday evening," Zelensky said.
"Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude towards everything that is happening."
He called on allies to keep up "real pressure" on Moscow and for more air defence supplies.
Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022 in what it hoped would be a swift attack to topple Zelensky and seize land.

Instead it has become bogged down in Europe's biggest conflict since World War II. Hundreds of thousands have been killed, millions forced from their homes and much of eastern and southern Ukraine destroyed.
Zelensky had met with Witkoff in Norway a day before the US-Russia talks in a meeting that came after days of spiralling Washington-Kyiv tensions.
In recent days, Trump has blocked new sanctions on Russia, struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, and called for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Zelensky has backed resuming trilateral talks -- several rounds of which over the last 18 months have failed to move the sides closer to a deal.

Russia is demanding Ukraine pull out of territory in the eastern Donetsk region that it still controls, and wants sweeping political and military restrictions on the size of its army and Western alliances.
Ukraine rejects the demands as tantamount to capitulation that would leave it exposed to a fresh attack.
The Kremlin said Witkoff had briefed Putin on "some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv" from the Oslo meeting, but that "there wasn't really much substance in them".
Moscow also said that a summit between Trump, Putin and China's Xi was being prepared in China for next month, with Europeans and Ukraine worrying a deal could be struck over their heads.
Shortly after hosting Witkoff on Wednesday, Putin held talks with Chinese premier Li Qiang, who was visiting Saint Petersburg.
Witkoff said on social media the talks with Putin were "constructive" but that "there is still important work left to do".
Discussions would continue between the United States, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level, he added.
Putin has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine -- either through a deal or on the battlefield.
7a5dff398a4c13fb: In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit.

On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality, and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out.

Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we've gone over it no matter which records you choose.

At 6 pm, the ringgit eased to 4.0815/0850 against the greenback from yesterday’s close of 4.0790/0825.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said market participants’ reassessment of next week’s FOMC decision drove movements in the US DXY, with traders likely to focus on the accompanying FOMC statement for clues on a possible rate hike in December.
“In that sense, support for the DXY is still visible, and the US dollar-ringgit pair could continue to trade within a narrow range,” he said.
At the close, the ringgit traded lower against a basket of major currencies.

It decreased versus the Japanese yen to 2.6035/6057 from 2.5790/5814 at Wednesday’s close; it declined against the British pound to 5.4659/4706 from 5.4642/4689, and it inched down vis-a-vis the euro to 4.5790/5830 from 4.5770/5810.
The ringgit performed mostly higher against its Asean peers.

It gained versus the Thai baht to 12.0973/1120 from 12.1287/1434 at yesterday’s close, appreciated against the Indonesian rupiah to 225.9/226.3 from 226.2/226.7 and strengthened vis-a-vis the Philippine peso to 6.42/6.43 from 6.44/6.45.
The ringgit eased against the Singapore dollar to 3.1959/1992 from 3.1917/1947 at yesterday’s close. — Bernama
45d572927c8e61ec: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Perikatan Nasional (PN) chairman Datuk Seri Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar has welcomed a High Court ruling granting an interim stay against the Registrar of Societies’ (RoS) decision to deregister the coalition, saying it will now direct its full electoral machinery towards the Melaka state election.

In a statement today, Ahmad Samsuri said that PN was “on the right path in defending our rights through legal channels” and maintained that political adversaries seeking to “erase” the coalition would fail to undermine its resolve.

“PN remains steadfast, and this struggle will continue,” he said, offering gratitude to supporters for their prayers and commending the coalition’s legal team for securing the urgent court intervention.

Earlier today, High Court Judge Datuk Azizan Md Arshad allowed PN’s leave application to stay the RoS order revoking the coalition’s corporate registration pending the final disposal of its substantive judicial review challenge.
The court concurrently froze the enforcement of an accompanying RoS directive that had ordered the immediate suspension of all PN operations nationwide.

The interim stay removes a legal cloud hovering over the coalition, allowing PN to operate unhindered as an approved political entity and field candidates under its official logo for the Melaka state election set for Nov 14.

With the legal hurdle cleared, Ahmad Samsuri instructed the coalition’s grassroots wings to pivot immediately from courtroom battles to the ballot box, rallying party workers to “strengthen preparations, foster closer cooperation and present the best offerings to the people.”
“We shall continue to move forward,” he said.
d75d242b9f2d3338: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Local application developers can leverage open public transport data to help commuters plan their journeys more conveniently, Transport Minister Anthony Loke said.

“Data under the ministry’s purview mainly relates to public transport, while road-related data involves other agencies, including the Works Ministry and the Public Works Department.
“Prasarana Malaysia Berhad (Prasarana) has made various datasets available to the public, covering daily passenger numbers, train frequency and service schedules,” he said.

At the event, Loke launched Phase Three of the Masjid Jamek LRT Station beautification project, which involves a RM5 million investment by Prasarana to improve commuter comfort and the station environment.

6864150b6dbf5f8f: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 22 — Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) staff have been urged to uphold integrity and good governance to preserve public trust in the country’s communications institution.

Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) Chief Commissioner Datuk Seri Abd Halim Aman said MCMC staff should have the courage to report any abuse of power or unlawful instructions through official channels.

“Have the courage to stand up for what is right and report any misconduct. Wrongdoing must never be covered up,” he said in his address at the MCMC 2026 Integrity and Audit Month closing ceremony, details of which were shared on the MACC’s Facebook page today.
Abd Halim said MCMC’s integrity programmes showed that both its senior management and staff were committed to strengthening accountability.
He said integrity went beyond compliance with written rules and audit requirements, stemming instead from personal values and principles, especially when honesty and trustworthiness were tested.
“Everyone must uphold the trust placed in them, regardless of their rank or position, and authority must not be treated as a privilege.

Others in attendance included MCMC commissioner General (Rtd) Tan Sri Zulkifeli Mohd Zin, MCMC managing director Abdul Karim Fakir Ali and Malaysian Anti-Corruption Academy senior director Datuk Mohamad Zamri Zainul Abidin.
Meanwhile, Mohamad Salmi said MCMC remained committed to curbing corruption and ensuring that accountable governance systems were consistently implemented.
“MCMC strives to ensure that the benefits of every fund it manages are returned to the people in a transparent and orderly manner,” he said. — Bernama
00bb17bb6751ebb5: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Two men who went viral on social media after crashing into public vehicles while attempting to evade police in Bukit Antarabangsa were charged in three separate courts in Ampang today on various offences, including obstructing civil servants, possessing dangerous weapons and drugs.

Private driver Muhammad Putra Zulfaiz Zaidi, 32, and mechanic Mohamad Danial Haiqal Kamal Arifin, 21, pleaded not guilty to all charges read before Sessions Court Judge Norshila Kamarudin and Magistrates Siti Nur Ain Ariffin and Tiong Wen Wen.

Before Judge Norshila Kamarudin, the two friends were jointly charged with possessing dangerous weapons in a public place, namely a machete and a sickle, at Jalan Wangsa 5, Bukit Antarabangsa, at 11 am on Oct 11.

The charge is framed under Section 6(1) of the Corrosive and Explosive Substances and Offensive Weapons Act 1958, read together with Section 34 of the Penal Code, which provides for imprisonment between five and 10 years, as well as caning.

Meanwhile, before Magistrate Siti Nur Ain, the duo faced two charges of obstructing police duties under Section 186 of the Penal Code, read together with Section 34 of the Penal Code, which carries imprisonment of up to two years or a fine of up to RM10,000, or both.

On the first charge, both men are accused of obstructing Cpl Muhammad Azfar Abdul Rahman and Lance Cpl Muhammad Yashar Hassan by fleeing in an Isuzu D-Max four-wheel-drive at Jalan Wangsa 5 at 11 am on Oct 11. The second charge involves Cpl Mohamad Syisyi Pauzi at Jalan Wangsa 1 at 5.30 am on Oct 10.
In the same court, Muhammad Putra Zulfaiz was charged individually with driving the four-wheel-drive with a false registration number under the Road Transport Act 1987.

He was also charged with consuming amphetamine and methamphetamine at the Ampang Jaya District Police Headquarters’ Narcotics Criminal Investigation Division office at 10.45 pm on Oct 11, under Section 15(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952.

Before Magistrate Tiong, they were jointly charged with driving the vehicle dangerously at the same location and time under Section 42(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987, read together with Section 34 of the Penal Code, which provides for a maximum of five years’ imprisonment and a fine of between RM5,000 and RM15,000.

They were also charged under Section 29(1) of the Minor Offences Act 1955 for failing to give a reasonable explanation for the possession of suspicious items, including two slings, a metal lock, an adjustable wrench, wire cutters, a steel hammer, a crowbar and chisel blades.
Also before Magistrate Tiong, Mohamad Danial Haiqal was charged individually with consuming amphetamine and methamphetamine on the same date and at the same location as Muhammad Putra Zulfaiz.
In the proceedings before Magistrate Siti Nur Ain, the court granted Muhammad Putra Zulfaiz bail of RM13,000, while Mohamad Danial Haiqal was granted bail of RM8,000 with one surety.
However, Judge Norshila and Magistrate Tiong did not grant bail to either accused due to the absence of a surety at today’s proceedings. All courts fixed Nov 26 for mention.
Deputy public prosecutors M. Ramanathan Alias Ashwin, Muhammad Aizudin Radthuan and Nadiah Malek Fauzie appeared for the prosecution.
Muhammad Putra Zulfaiz was represented by lawyer Daneish Thayalan and Mohamad Danial Haiqal by National Legal Aid Foundation lawyer Ernie Ahmad.

On Oct 11, police arrested both suspects after the vehicle they were travelling in crashed into several other private vehicles before being intercepted at the Jalan Jelatek–Jalan Taman Setiawangsa intersection here. — Bernama
1afbec52ef91fbbe: MELAKA, Oct 22 — Police crippled the activities of two call center syndicates suspected of being involved in online non-existent investment scams and love scams through two separate operations around Melaka Raya and Ayer Keroh, here.

Melaka Tengah District Police Chief ACP Halim Abas said that in the first operation on October 20, 14 Chinese nationals - comprising 11 men and three women aged between 21 and 52 - were arrested at four accommodation units in a hotel in Melaka Raya between 1pm and 3 pm.
“Initial investigations found that the premises were suspected of being used as a call center operations hub for online non-existent investment scam activities targeting Chinese nationals.

“The syndicate is believed to have started operating since mid-September, with the suspects acting as customer service officers to find and contact victims, as well as receiving a salary of about RM3,000,” he said at a press conference here today.

Halim added that police also seized 28 mobile phones of various brands, two laptops, a tablet, a translation device, five mobile phone farm charging/control hubs, 96 prepaid SIM cards, and RM6,400 in cash, with the total value of the seizures estimated at RM43,500.

Meanwhile, he said that in the second operation yesterday at about 3:00 pm, a premises at a resort around Ayer Keroh was raided, leading to the arrest of 15 men consisting of 14 Vietnamese nationals and one Chinese national aged between 21 and 40.

“Initial investigations found that the premises were suspected of being used as a call center operations hub for online scam activities using a love scam modus operandi targeting Vietnamese nationals.

“The syndicate is believed to have started operating since the beginning of this month, with the suspects playing the role of customer service officers to find and contact victims, as well as receiving a salary of about RM2,500,” he said.

Halim said police seized 11 sets of computers of various brands, 24 mobile phones, a Starlink router, a remote control set, a translation device, and 15 passport books, with the total value of the seizures estimated at RM43,400.
He added that four investigation papers were opened regarding the first operation, while one investigation paper was opened for the second operation.
All suspects are being investigated under Section 420 of the Penal Code as well as Section 6(1)© of the Immigration Act 1959/63 for offences related to personal identification documents.

“All suspects in the first operation have been remanded for four days from October 21 to 24, while the suspects in the second operation have been remanded for four days from October 22 to 25 to assist with the investigation,” he said. — Bernama
47f9432a28fb5645: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 22 — The Court of Appeal today overturned a High Court decision that had released a wheelchair-bound man on bail pending the disposal of his drug trafficking trial.

A three-man bench led by Justice Datuk Choo Kah Sing, alongside K. Muniandy and Datuk Seri Latifah Mohd Tahar, allowed the prosecution’s appeal to set aside the High Court’s ruling and ordered M. Alagesan to be remanded in custody.
Justice Choo, who delivered the unanimous decision, however, granted the defence’s application for Alagesan to be placed at the Sungai Buloh Hospital until the conclusion of his trial.
He held that the High Court judge erred in applying Section 388 of the Criminal Procedure Code to allow bail when there is an express law dealing with bail for drug trafficking offences.

He said the High Court’s decision was against the provision of Section 41B (1) (a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act, which states that bail shall not be granted to an accused person charged under the Act with an offence punishable by death or life imprisonment with not less than 12 strokes of the cane.
Justice Choo said Section 2 of the same Act stated that this subsection shall have the effect notwithstanding any written laws or any rule of law to the contrary.
The court ordered the RM150,000 bail deposited to be returned and revoked all previously imposed bail conditions.
“This court ordered the trial court to fix an early hearing date to complete the trial by the end of this year if possible considering the health condition of the accused,” Justice Choo said.

Earlier, lawyer Datuk Naran Singh, assisted by Amrick Singh Sandu, told the court that the trial dates have been scheduled for Feb 17 to 19 and March 24 to 26, 2027, and requested the court to issue a directive for the trial to be heard earlier.
Alagesan, 44, was charged with trafficking in 6.276 kg of cannabis at a house in Kg KL Tin Kalumpang, Kuala Kubu Baru, Hulu Selangor, Selangor on Feb 7, 2024.

On Sept 23, 2024, the Shah Alam High Court allowed Alagesan’s application to be released on bail pending disposal of his trial with RM150,000 with two sureties and imposed additional conditions including reporting to the nearest police station, surrendering his passport, and remaining at home from 7 pm to 7 am.

During proceedings, deputy public prosecutor Hafizah Johor Ariff Johor argued that Section 41B(1)(a) establishes a mandatory restriction that completely denies the right to bail for offences carrying the death penalty under the Dangerous Drugs Act, thereby divesting the High Court of any discretionary power to release the accused on bail pending completion of the trial.

She said that the High Court’s decision to grant bail in this case is a departure from established legal principles and it would open the door for thousands of detainees facing charges under Section 39B of the Dangerous Drug Act to apply for bail on subjective health grounds, thereby crippling Parliament’s intention to combat serious drug crimes.
In response, Naran Singh contended that despite the statutory prohibition under Section 41B, the court retains the inherent power to grant bail under exceptional circumstances.
He said Alagesan was paralysed from the waist down and was unable to squat, noting that standard prison toilets are equipped with squatting facilities. — Bernama

3b1852bb0011105e: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes.

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know.

The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling.

This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents.

Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.”
This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis.
Full Transcript
Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.
This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis.

Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized.
Two words for you: context matters.
My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis.
Welcome, Devavrat.
Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here.

Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale?

Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises.

The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision.

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come.

Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play?

Devavrat: Fantastic. Let’s just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let’s for a second imagine that all these, as they’re called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that’s happened in the universe and it’s likely to happen in the universe is all there.

Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one.

In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company’s doom.

Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we’re talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization?

Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that’s where their primary, let’s call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better.

Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that’s where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision.
Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that’s the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer?

Devavrat: That’s a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it’s the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they’re consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate.

Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we’re talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that.

Devavrat: It’s again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it’s just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don’t need to be complete. They don’t need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic’s architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it.

And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis’s infrastructure, so it’s not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let’s say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor’s software that’s coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it.

Megan: Right. So that’s the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two?

Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they’re doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that’s where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won’t be doing that.

On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don’t have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that’s where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it’s organization’s role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go.

And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that’s where people will have to spend time.

The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it’s difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we’ll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner.
Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well?

Devavrat: Okay, that’s a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let’s identify the process around it. Let’s identify each step of the process. Let’s take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let’s try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let’s measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that’ll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that’s one.

Second is governance. Well, we’re going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this.

And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it’s really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there’s a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed.

Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn’t it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you’re simply most excited about?

Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They’re all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that’s one.

Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that’s spent in coordination, that’s why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak.

And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that’s a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.

5c0cd6c286dc148a: How much do you know about permafrost?
Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.

The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two in-depth stories about permafrost. His reporting took him to the boreal forests of Alaska, where he helicoptered into the wilderness to learn more about how this material could affect our climate both now and in the future.

I’d recommend you give both of James’s stories a read. There’s this feature about efforts to tackle the intensifying fires that are threatening permafrost, as well as this look at how researchers are trying to understand the complicated tangle of potential climate effects. Here are three things I took away.
Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change

Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere. While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age.

That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years. But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change. Those emissions form a feedback loop, accelerating warming further.
The steady rise in global temperatures has already shrunk the footprint of the Arctic permafrost by about 12% since 1850, and the pace has been picking up in the last 50 years.

The wild thing is, only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost. And none of them include the abrupt thaw and collapse that can happen after events like heat waves and fires (more on those fires in a moment). There are efforts to make sure future UN reports reflect the growing science, but for now, all this means that we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm.
Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss

Fire is a natural part of boreal forests’ life cycle, but they’re getting more intense because of climate change. And crucially, fires can accelerate the thawing of permafrost. By the end of the century, this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada and Alaska is generally to let wildfires burn as long as they’re not threatening human habitats. But some researchers say we should explore fighting these fires to save the carbon trapped in the forests and the permafrost beneath them.

Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, essentially highlighting areas where fires are most likely to spread and which areas are home to certain types of permafrost that would release the most emissions. (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost. Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form from the late Pleistocene era.)

That’s all just the beginning—once we figure out potential targets, the question is what to do about it. Some suggest setting more prescribed fires, something Indigenous groups have done for thousands of years, partly to reduce the danger of massive blazes. Or resources could go to early detection and efforts to put out fires before they grow.
The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated

There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere. We know that permafrost thawing can release greenhouse-gas emissions and drive climate change. But there are complications.

One particularly big wrinkle: Other effects from permafrost thawing and fire recovery might counteract the carbon lost from those events. For example, as temperatures warm, plants can gradually move north and take hold where they couldn’t have before. Those plants soak up carbon from the atmosphere as they grow, at least partly locking away what was emitted.

Researchers are working to better understand this ecosystem. And the more we learn, the more complicated the picture looks. How much carbon is lost from permafrost, and how much a given area will recover its carbon, depend on a huge array of factors. How severe are the fires that have accelerated local thawing? What’s the local climate and environment? And what kind of permafrost is at stake?
The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand.

4d49c47173fedd24: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 22 — Wawasan information chief and Machang MP Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal has urged Putrajaya to maintain Digital Nasional Bhd’s (DNB) Western technology stack, saying it is needed to balance the growing role of Chinese technology in Malaysia’s 5G and AI infrastructure.
Wan Fayhsal made the call in the Dewan Rakyat while Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who is also the Tambun MP, was present in the chamber.
He said DNB’s Ericsson-based network was now Malaysia’s main Western technology counterweight, following U Mobile’s selection of Huawei for the country’s second 5G network.

He said the need to retain that balance had become more pressing as the government considers Huawei’s Ascend 910C chips for its proposed sovereign AI cloud, which could eventually handle sensitive government data.
“DNB was established by the Perikatan Nasional government in 2021. Now there are two paths, namely DNB with Ericsson and U Mobile with Huawei,” he said during his Budget 2027 debate.
“This is a good thing because Malaysia can benefit from Western and Eastern technology, as stressed by Tambun previously.”
Wan Fayhsal said Malaysia should not allow one technology ecosystem to become dominant across its critical digital infrastructure.

“I hope the government can retain both systems because, in my discussions with ambassadors from Europe and other Western countries, they want Malaysia to provide truly sovereign digital infrastructure so that they can invest in sensitive sectors,” he said.

The MP said keeping DNB on Western technology was therefore about more than 5G coverage or speed. It would give Malaysia and foreign investors a credible alternative for operations involving sensitive data.
He said the government’s proposed sovereign AI cloud made this consideration more urgent.

The government had announced a proposed RM2 billion allocation through the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) to establish the cloud under Budget 2026, with the initiative repeated in Budget 2027.
Wan Fayhsal said Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil had stated that work was under way to protect government data.
“Huawei Ascend 910C chips are being considered, and Telekom Malaysia (TM) has been selected to manage this project,” he said.
“The question is whether the government has carried out a risk assessment on the suppliers who will be used to handle national data.
“How will the government manage sensitivities related to digital sovereignty?”
He said the issue was whether Malaysia was building enough safeguards and alternatives as Chinese technology takes a greater role in the country’s digital ecosystem.
“The minister said work is ongoing to protect government data,” he said. “The government must explain whether it has conducted a risk assessment of the suppliers.”

Wan Fayhsal did not call for Chinese technology to be excluded. Instead, he said Malaysia should preserve both Western and Chinese technology pathways, so the country is not dependent on any one supplier or geopolitical bloc.
“Malaysia can benefit from Western and Eastern technology,” he said.

Maintaining DNB’s Ericsson-based stack, he added, would ensure that Malaysia retains a meaningful Western option while U Mobile’s Huawei-backed 5G network and the proposed sovereign AI cloud expand the role of Chinese technology in critical national infrastructure.

27a4538a956d6533: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 22 — Malaysia will introduce several transformative measures to strengthen efforts to tackle transboundary haze when it chairs the Sub-Regional Ministerial Steering Committee (MSC) on Transboundary Haze Pollution next year.

Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Datuk Seri Arthur Joseph Kurup said his ministry was conducting studies and drafting several new initiatives to ensure more effective and concrete action to address the recurring haze problem.
“Malaysia will take over the MSC chairmanship next year, and we are studying and planning several new initiatives to strengthen Asean-level efforts to tackle the haze problem.
“We hope to take more effective and concrete measures when we chair the MSC,” he told a press conference on the latest haze situation here today.

He said Malaysia proposed two key initiatives at the Asean ministerial meeting on July 9: science diplomacy, to ensure planning, action and spending to tackle haze are based on scientific data, enabling more targeted fire prevention and suppression efforts, and the setting up of a sustainable haze fund.
“The proposed sustainable haze fund, if approved, would serve as an Asean-level mechanism to help member states strengthen prevention, preparedness and monitoring measures,” he said.

He said most fires involved extremely dry peatland, where they could spread underground undetected for weeks or months, highlighting the need to study new technologies, including dry ice-based methods, to improve firefighting efforts.

In a related development, Arthur said Malaysia had also introduced the Malaysian Community Multiscale Air Quality Model (CMAQ), which can forecast potential air pollution and haze up to five days in advance.
He said the Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) had developed the platform to provide detailed air quality forecasts for Malaysia and the wider Southeast Asian region.

“We hope other countries will also adopt the system so that the public can plan and prepare up to five days in advance,” he said, adding that the platform began operating this year and is open to the public and Asean member states.

On the haze situation, Arthur said the transition to the Northeast Monsoon, expected to begin in late October, could alter the movement of transboundary haze currently affecting several areas in the south of the country, particularly Sarawak and Johor.

He said shifts in wind direction during the Northeast Monsoon could carry haze to other areas, easing its impact on areas currently affected, noting that haze drifting northwards from the south had significantly affected southern Sarawak, Johor and Singapore.

However, Arthur said Malaysia faced a greater risk of transboundary haze as the Super El Niño phenomenon was forecast to intensify from this month until January 2027, increasing the likelihood of forest and peatland fires in the region.

He said the El Niño phenomenon is expected to persist until mid-2027, with the year potentially among the hottest on record, bringing increasingly erratic rainfall, a higher risk of drought and more hotspots and fires that could worsen the haze.

“We also forecast that next year could be among the hottest on record, with temperature anomalies exceeding 2°C,” he said, adding that the government had taken into account the experience of the 2015-2016 Super El Niño, when rainfall decreased by up to 30 per cent in peninsular Malaysia and 45 per cent in Sabah.
He said prolonged hot and dry conditions would not only increase the risk of forest and peatland fires but could also affect agriculture, food security, water supplies and public health. — Bernama

8cacaf29b1375238: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.

What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning.
As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it

Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind.

Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip.

And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade.

A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more.

“You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention.
Matching storage to the AI data life cycle

Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer.

This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage
What this means for how AI gets budgeted

For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators.

Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished.

A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand.
Building for economically scalable capacity

Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it.

What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives.

Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales.
There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget:
What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it?
Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing?
If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse?
Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence. That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after.

3cf55decbd424670: Indian certification authority eMudhra has defended the laughably weak private keys it used to sign some digital certificates it issued, and suggested others should share the blame for the incident.

In case you’re coming to this one late, news broke yesterday that private keys the company used to sign certs were beyond weak: one was literally just the number “4,” and several others were short strings of easily guessed two-or-three-digit numbers. It’s easy to deduce the value of those keys, which makes it possible to forge certs and impersonate websites or other resources.

That’s gold for scammers, phishers, and other miscreants. The entire infosec industry has pointed that out, urged swift adoption of better certs, and lamented the fact that implementing replacements will be a long and thankless task.
eMudhra’s statement about the incident says it generated keys during “a Key Generation Ceremony (KGC) held on April 30, 2025, using FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Hardware Security Modules (HSMs).”
Such hardware is the standard kit for the job and should in theory produce nicely complex keys and store them securely.

“A flaw in the KGC caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the statement claims. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores. eMudhra is working to establish the root cause.”
The company then gets a tad defensive.

“These roots and issuing CAs have gone through independent audits for two years in a row and have been in browser trust lists since mid-2025,” the statement adds, seemingly shifting some blame to auditors and other stakeholders.
The announcement then points out that eMudhra’s TLS business generates just one percent of its revenue, meaning this mess won’t impact its bottom line too much.
That’s nice to know for the company’s investors but rather misses the point that whoever relies on the company now has an urgent, unwanted, and costly job to do replacing certs.

“eMudhra is working directly with customers who may be affected to give them replacement certificates, so that critical services are not disrupted. The company is also working with the root programs and continues its root-cause investigation,” the statement adds.
The company allows that the incident “may have some reputational risks on eMudhra which cannot be quantified.”

“It’s a simple question for any enterprise. Would you like something that’s 10 percent of the cost if it’s 90 percent as good as the best, or do you want to pay that 10 times higher cost?”
Krishna thinks businesses will most often choose not to incur the higher costs.

“Then the question is: how many tasks require that? I would tell you some do, but the vast majority, summarizing an email, examining a contract, answering a customer call, composing an email, all of those can be done as well with the much cheaper answer.”

The CEO said those numbers mean IBM is seeing booming interest in on-prem AI infrastructure. While he thinks most businesses can build useful AI infrastructure in just two or three racks, he feels many will struggle to get it running.

“The question becomes: how do you do that?” he said. “The question that the enterprise struggles with is: ‘Where are my kernel engineers? Where are the people who worry about the underlying network? Who can make sure that the model is clustered on GPUs that are close to each other in network proximity? Who can make sure that you’re doing the right caching of results so you get an incredible response?’”

He didn’t have answers, other than to say IBM will produce software that eases AI deployments. Krishna also predicted demand for on-prem AI will spur sales of Big Blue’s Spyre mainframe accelerator cards.

The CEO said current-gen z17 mainframes have delivered $1bn more revenue than any previous model, and said Big Blue’s new rackable models delivered “the strongest midrange launch in IBM Z in nearly two decades.” Mainframe revenue, however, fell 20 percent – as IBM expects given it’s now 18 months since it launched the z17.
IBM’s infrastructure revenue grew five percent year-over-year to $3.7 billion, much slower improvement than recorded by rivals Dell, HPE, and Lenovo.

Software did rather better, scoring nine percent growth to reach $7.8 billion for the quarter. Red Hat was the star, growing eleven percent and increasing annual recurring revenue by 30 percent. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. That’s a solid result for a product line launched in 2024, and IBM believes there’s more to come given the possibility some VMware users are on the move.
Total quarterly revenue hit $17.1 billion, up five percent. IBM’s share price wobbled in after-hours trading and ended down a point or two.

Another IBM matter The Register is watching today is a severity one incident in the Big Blue cloud, caused by “emergency maintenance” that meant users could not provision new resources or virtual private clouds for 90 minutes. Users of IBM’s Classic Cloud, the service it acquired from SoftLayer in 2013, have been told Big Blue will “restore new provisioning and resource management in our Classic environment” by 08:00 UTC on Thursday – meaning the incident will last at least 16 hours.

IBM commenced that work a handful of hours after the announcement of critical bugs in PHP. We’ve asked if fixing that flaw is the reason for the incident and will update this story if we get a response. ®
